paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.1:1 Rule 13.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.1. In D'Amico v. Wiemkin, 2010 ABQB 785, 2010 CarswellAlta 2539, 497 A.R. 360, 47 Alta. L.R. (5th) 414, 5 C.P.C. (7th) 92, the first trial judge in an action which arose out of a motor vehicle accident reserved his decision after a total of seven weeks of trial Prior to rendering his decision, the first trial judge concluded that “it was impossible for him to continue to judgment and that therefore he was compelled to recuse himself.” The action was reassigned to Mr. Justice Jeffrey and the question before him was whether he had to rehear all the witnesses or if he could proceed on the basis of transcripts of the evidence led before the first trial judge. The application was made under the previous Rule 391, but Jeffrey, J. commented on Rule 13.1. At paragraphs 36–39: 36 Although this application was brought and heard pursuant to the old rules, given the recent coming into force of new court rules in Alberta (Alberta Rules of Court, A.R. 124/2010), a comment on the new is warranted. The comparable new rule, Rule 13.1, has different wording than the old Rule 391. Rule 13.1 says that in circumstances such as these, the new judge “may act in place of or replace another judge”. 37 Principles of statutory interpretation suggest that each of these terms (“in place of” and “replace”) are not to be ascribed the same meaning; the legislators would not have repeated themselves, using two terms for the same thing where one would suffice [See, for example, Pigeon, L-P. Drafting and Interpreting Legislation. Toronto, Ontario: The Carswell Co. Ltd.; 1988, at p. 46]. I need not decide the meaning or effect of each of these two distinct terms within this application, but will observe that for “in place of” to mean something other than “replace” it likely refers to filling in for the first judge, just not permanently as implied by “replace”. It could be for a specific step or task that the successor acts “in place of” the former; it could be for a set period of time. But at the conclusion of that task or time period the actions of the successor judge cease before the completion of the matter. Like the old Rule 391, its breadth seems to permit but not require the successor to pick up where the first left off, such as here at the end of the first trial record, and continue on to conclusion. 38 I note further that the new Rule 6.10 contemplates an “electronic hearing.” In an electronic hearing the parties and the judge can all hear each other, but not see each other. The Rule further provides that, on application, the electronic hearing can be ordered by the court in the absence of consent of the parties. 39 Subsection 18(3) of the Interpretation Act is more conclusive on the threshold issue. In my view it more clearly grants to the successor judge the power to pick-up where the predecessor left off regardless of the consent of any of the litigants. It says, again in part: “… the proceeding, matter or thing … may be continued or completed before any other judge of the same court.” Both the terms “completed” and “continued”, but particularly “continued”, imply carrying on from where the matter was left, not restarting from the beginning.

paragraphs.text: 13.4. Counting months and years

sentences.text: Counting months and years

paragraphs.text: (1) When counting to or from a date in months, time is calculated from the date on which the event or activity occurs in the month to the same-numbered day in a subsequent or previous month, as the case requires. (2) If the count ends on the 29th, 30th or 31st and there is no same-numbered date in the subsequent or previous month, the count ends on the last day of the subsequent or previous month, as the case requires. (3) When counting to or from an event or activity in years, time is calculated from the date on which the activity or event occurs in a year to the same-numbered date in a subsequent or previous year, as the case requires. (4) If the count starts on February 29th and ends in a year that is not a leap year, the count ends on February 28th of that year. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 23

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the Court otherwise orders or a rule otherwise provides, the parties may agree to extend any time period specified in these rules. (2) The Court may, unless a rule otherwise provides, stay, extend or shorten a time period that is (a) specified in these rules, (b) specified in an order or judgment, or (c) agreed on by the parties. (3) The order to extend or shorten a time period may be made whether or not the period has expired.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.5:1 Rule 13.5 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.5. 1. Law Under Previous Rule Applies In Pagnucco (Next Friend of) v. Sears Canada Inc., 2011 ABQB 810, 2011 CarswellAlta 2298 (Master), the Defendant brought an application to extend the time within which a Third Party Notice could be filed. Master Schlosser found that the law as developed under the old rule still applied, and said, at paragraphs 9–15: 9 Rule 13.5 allows the Court to extend time. The factors to be considered are: 1. the length of delay; 2. the explanation for the delay; 3. the relative prejudice to the parties. 10 The test is flexible. An absence of an explanation for the delay may not be, in and of itself, fatal to the application. (Dean (below) para. 66 and Flight v. Dillon, [2001] AJ No. 329, per Moreau J.) 11 There is also authority to suggest that a late Third Party claim must have an “air of reality”: Condominium Corp. No. 9813678 v. Statesman Corp., 2008 ABQB 495 per Wittmann, ACJ (as he then was) para. 46 (and the cases cited there). The reason for this latter requirement is that the Court will not act without purpose. There is little purpose in allowing a late proceeding that is bound to fail. 12 The most important factors are whether there is serious prejudice or inexcusable delay. If the delay is significant, evidence is required to explain it: Lister v. Calgary (City), (1997) 47 Alta. LR (3d) 14 (CA) at para. 9; Hein v. Barrett, 2008 ABQB 548 per Hanebury, M. (at para. 23), which contains a helpful review of the main points. 13 In this case, the first hurdle is whether a limitation has expired. If it is plain and obvious, or beyond doubt that the limitation has expired, there is no point in allowing the Third Party Notice to be filed as it would just be struck out. Campbell v. Calgary (City) Police Service, 2009 ABQB 58; Alliance Pipeline Ltd. Partnership v. C.E. Franklin Ltd. 2007 ABQB 582; Dean v. Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412 (QB), per Slatter J. (as he then was). If there is reasonable doubt that the limitation has expired, and all of the other elements of the test are satisfied, the Third Party claim can proceed while preserving the Third Party's rights to raise a limitations defence. Anderson v. Airsprint Inc.. 2005 ABCA 332, para. 15. 14 Limitations are one of the factors to be considered in determining the relative prejudice to the parties. The ability to start a new claim is apparently a reason for not allowing a Third Party action. Conversely, the loss of a right to start a new action apparently can weigh in favour of a late Third Party Notice. (Dean at para. 58 and the cases cited there). 15 There is no reason to think that this law has changed under the new Rules. In Keef v. Peters, 2015 ABCA 16, 2015 CarswellAlta 24, Mr. Justice Brown said, at paragraph 6: [6] While an appellant must file his or her factum on time or the Registrar will strike the appeal (rules 14.23(1) and 14.24(1)), this Court retains discretion to extend time periods specified in the Rules of Court: rules 1.4(2)(h) and 13.5(2). The pertinent factors to consider in deciding whether to do so are (1) the reason for the delay, (2) the prospects of moving ahead with the appeal, (3) the prejudice to the other party, and (4) the potential merit of the appeal: Bowles v Beamish, 2009 ABCA 243 (CanLII) at para 6, 178 ACWS (3d) 298. In Coleman v. Coleman, 2014 ABCA 452, 2014 CarswellAlta 2388, 9 Alta. L.R. (6th) 367, 62 C.P.C. (7th) 425, Justice Wakeling held that R. 13.5(2) applies to a deadline in Part 14 “unless there is an express declaration that it does not.” At paragraphs 26–29, his Lordship said: [26] Rule 13.5(2) gives this Court jurisdiction to extend the six-month time period in r. 14.47 unless another rule “otherwise provides”. [27] What does “otherwise provides” mean? [28] Is this disqualifying condition met only by an express declaration that r. 13.5(2) does not apply to a specific role? If so, r 13.5(2) would appear to apply to deadlines except those embedded in rr. 3.15(2), 3.27(2) and 4.33(4) of the Alberta Rules of Court. Rule 3.15(2) provides that “an originating application for judicial review to set aside a decision or act of a person or body must be filed and served within 6 months after the date of decision or act, and rule 13.5 … does not apply to this time period”. [29] I am satisfied that r. 13.5(2) applies to a deadline in Part 14 unless there is an express declaration that it does not.[16] Part 14, read as a discrete unit and in conjunction with the other parts of the Alberta Rules of Court, reveals a commitment to Court control over its own process. A contrary conclusion would be inconsistent with that underlying purpose. 2. Appeal Period In considering whether to extend the time for appealing or not this division has, since 1931, followed its judgment in Cairns v. Cairns, [1931] 26 Alta. L.R. 69 … The summary of this judgment, contained in the headnote, was approved in Ramsdell v. Elliott and U.S. Fidelity and Guaranty Co., [1937] 1 W.W.R. 37 (Alta. C.A.), by McGillivray J.A., who had given the judgment of the majority in Cairns v. Cairns. This has led to some misunderstanding of the judgment apparently, not only by members of the bar of Alberta, but by other courts in other provinces. The relevant portion of the [W.W.R.] headnote reads: Where a person has recovered a judgment and the time for giving notice of appeal therefrom has expired he has a vested interest in the judgment and in the benefits which may flow from it that will not lightly be interfered with by the Courts. Therefore an extension of time within which to give notice of appeal will not be granted as a matter of course, but a heavy burden rests on the applicant of showing cause why the indulgence of the court should be extended to him. It is incumbent upon him: (1) To show that a bona-fide intention to appeal was entertained while the right to appeal existed and that the failure to appeal was by reason of some special circumstance which served to excuse or justify such failure; (2) To account for the delay and to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust, having regard to the position of both parties, to disturb the judgment; (3) To show that he has not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal; (4) To show that he would have a reasonable chance of success if allowed to prosecute the appeal. Royal Bank v. Morin (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 127 at 128-29 (C.A.). Subsequent authority has made it clear that “compliance with all of the Cairns considerations is not necessary.” In Independent Acceptance Corp. v. Hautz (2008), 97 Alta. L.R. (4th) 307 (Q.B.), Justice Kent had before her an application to extend the period within which to file an appeal from a decision of the Provincial Court of Alberta. Counsel for the proposed appellant had misunderstood from whence one was to calculate the appeal period of 30 days, and consequently filed the notice of appeal ten days after the appeal period had expired. Her Ladyship, at pp. 313–314, discussed the test as set out in Cairns: 27 Applying the Cairns considerations to the facts of the case, the Court [in Royal Bank v. Morin (1977), 6 A.R. 341 (Alta. C.A.)] held at para. 21 that, despite the equivocal evidence, in the circumstances, “it would result in a grave miscarriage of justice not to extend the time for appeal.” Implicit in this conclusion is that, although the Cairns considerations are a useful template for judging whether it is appropriate to extend the time period within which one may give notice of appeal, they are not determinative. 28 The Court stressed at para. 17 that the English jurisprudence has taken the position that “the failure of a solicitor to fulfil an obligation to a client is not always a special circumstance justifying an extension of time for appealing.” This approach has not, however, been followed in Canada, as is evidenced by the Alberta Supreme Court, Appellate Division decision in Hudson v. Bower 1968 67 W.W.R. 564 Shewchuk, Re, 1 D.L.R. (3d) 288 Alta. S.C. (A.D.) (“Hudson”). 29 The facts in Hudson are virtually identical to the present case, in that the solicitor for the appellant mistakenly believed that the Rule extending the time for filing pleadings during vacation also applied to the filing of notices of appeal. The Court distinguished the English jurisprudence on the basis that English law required a special application with stringent requirements that Canadian law did not. Further, it held at para. 2 that: [w]hile solicitors are presumed to know the proper interpretation of the Rules of Court, experience has shown that his [or her] presumption is often not well founded. In the present case the delay was short and no prejudice was shown, and the appellant having shown a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, we have accordingly extended the time for appeal [sic]. 30 Ultimately, Canadian jurisprudence has not embraced English case law on this point, preferring instead a justice-based approach. The Court in Royal Bank explained at para. 17: [i]n many cases where the negligence is that of the solicitor in failing to file a notice of appeal the court may simply leave the client where he must look to the solicitor for compensation for the negligence in failing to file the notice. However, it is a circumstance that must be considered in deciding whether to extend time. The main consideration is not the position of the solicitor, but what would be the result to the litigants [emphasis added]. 31 Referring to the above observations, the late McGillivray C.J.A. affirmed in Smoky Lake General and Auxiliary Hospital and Nursing Home (District No. 73) v. Higdon (1983), 50 A.R. 185, 4 D.L.R. (4th) 175 (C.A.) (“Smoky Lake”) that courts should, in every case, take note of the Cairns considerations. That said, he stressed at para. 16 that courts “retain the unfettered discretion to extend the time for appealing if the justice of the situation so requires.” 32 The conclusions reached in Royal Bank and Smoky Lake were affirmed by the Court of Queen's Bench in Strilets v. Vicom Multimedia Inc. ((2000),), 274 A.R. 6, [2001] 1 W.W.R. 342 ((Q.B.)) (“Strilets”). The Court emphasized that, although the Cairns considerations are a useful guide, they remain merely considerations. Consequently, as is evidenced in the Royal Bank decision, compliance with all of the Cairns considerations is not necessary. 33 A further affirming example is found in Cascade Development Corp. v. Red Deer College (1991), 115 A.R. 325 (C.A.) (“Cascade”), in which the Court of Appeal held at para. 2 that it is neither necessary to show an absence of prejudice (Cairns consideration #2), nor a reasonable chance of success (Cairns consideration #4) in cases where the delay “is only a day or so.” Conclusion 34 The above case law suggests that the Alberta Court of Appeal and Court of Queen's Bench have relaxed the requirements set out in Cairns; the ultimate decision as to whether an extension will be granted, per Strilets at para. 46, “is basically on the Court's consideration of the interests of justice.” However, Mr. Justice Wakeling in Travis v. D & J Overhead Door Ltd., 2016 ABCA 319, 2016 CarswellAlta 2033 was of the view that there is “an onerous burden on those who wish to” extend the time within which to file an appeal. If his Lordship's view is shared by other members of the Court of Appeal, this case would seem to herald the beginning of an era in which it will be more difficult to obtain an order permitting the late filing of an appeal. Of particular note is his Lordship's comment that the litigant bore a duty to “monitor the steps” taken by his lawyer to file the appeal, and that the litigant “should have asked his lawyer to provide him with progress reports and pressed him to act” (paragraph 28, and also see paragraph 184). Justice Wakeling said (footnotes omitted): 5 In two decisions issued in the 1930s—Cairns v. Cairns, a 1931 judgment, and Ramsdell v. Elliott, a 1936 opinion, the Alberta Supreme Court Appellate Division laid the foundation for the test to be applied when assessing the merits of an application to extend the time for filing a notice of appeal. They recognize that an unappealed judgment or order is a valuable asset for the victorious party that should not be devalued “unless weighty reasons be given for asking the Court to interfere with that right”. The importance placed on the principle of finality prompted the Court to place a “heavy burden [on the applicant]… of showing cause why the indulgence of the Court should be granted”. The two judgments identified and confirmed six conditions that an applicant seeking leave to file a late notice of appeal must meet to secure the requested relief. 6 First, did the applicant form an intention to appeal while the right of appeal existed? 7 Second, has the applicant provided an explanation for the failure to file a timely appeal? 8 Third, if so, does this explanation constitute “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such failure”? 9 Fourth, has the applicant demonstrated that the delay has not “so seriously prejudiced [the respondent] as to make it unjust” to grant a time extension? 10 Fifth, has the applicant not taken the benefits of the judgment? 11 Sixth, it falls on the applicant to convince the court that “he had a reasonable chance of success if allowed to commence and prosecute the appeal”. 12 Stoddard v. Montague, a 2006 judgment, modified the old standard. The new formulation recognized that an applicant who demonstrated compliance with all six criteria was “generally” entitled to an extension. But now an applicant who missed one or more of the markers could still prevail “if there are ‘unique and special circumstances’ and it is in the interests of justice to [grant the extension]”. 13 In The Queen v. Canto, a 2015 judgment, the Court declared that “[t]hese [Cairns v. Cairns] factors guide the Court in exercising its discretion to extend the time to appeal, but they do not set rigid requirements, and they do not override the Court's general discretion to extend time in appropriate cases”. … 18 There is a presumption that an applicant who passes the six-part Cairns v. Cairns test and has filed a time-extension application as quickly as possible and seeks a very short extension—one measured in days—will be granted the requested relief. … 20 Exceptional circumstances exist if the applicant or counsel or both encounter events over which they have no control and make it impossible for them to protect the applicant's interests. A natural disaster—a fire or a flood that disrupts the normal operations of a law office—or an incapacitation, injury or illness that befalls the applicant or counsel are examples of events that qualify as exceptional circumstances. 21 But even the existence of exceptional circumstances does not eliminate the fundamental importance of the principle of finality and the need to validate the unimpeachable character of a decision not appealed within the prescribed appeal window or a relatively short time after it closes. There comes a point when the second appeal window must close. … 27 Mr. Travis' trial counsel claims that problems beyond his control prevented him from discharging his professional responsibilities. Without the opinion of a physician explaining the extent of the limitations the lawyer laboured under, I cannot conclude that Mr. Travis' lawyer's poor health prevented him from filing a notice of appeal. 28 Even if I accepted counsel's self-diagnosis and concluded that counsel's health prevented him from performing this task or realizing that he should withdraw, I would not have concluded that “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such failure” existed. Mr. Travis did next to nothing to monitor the steps his lawyer took to remedy the dismissal orders that were contrary to Mr. Travis' interests. Mr. Travis knew about the dismissal orders before his lawyer did. He was aware of the dilemma he faced from the very beginning. He should have asked his lawyer to provide him with progress reports and pressed him to act. … 48 Almost every reported Alberta judgment in the last seventy years dealing with an application to extend the time within which an applicant may file a notice of appeal cites Cairns v. Cairns, a 1931 decision of the Alberta Supreme Court Appellate Division. 49 It merits careful study. 50 Justice McGillivray wrote for a five-member panel. His judgment stands for four propositions. 51 First, a judgment that has not been appealed within the stipulated time frame is a valuable asset to the victorious party.24 “When the time for appealing has expired, the litigation is at an end; the successful party is entitled to the benefit of the judgment in his or her favour. At that stage, the successful party has a ‘vested right to retain the judgment’.” 52 Second, an unappealed decision is a final decision. Finality is so important that it ought to be disturbed only in extraordinary circumstances. Justice McGillivray held that “the holder of a judgment after the time for giving notice of appeal has expired, has a special right or interest which will not be set aside by the Courts, unless weighty reasons be given for asking the Court to interfere with that right”. 53 Lord Justice James, in International Financial Society (Ltd.) v. City of Moscow Gas Co., an 1878 judgment that Justice McGillivray cited, made it very clear that an extension would seldom be granted: The limitation of the time to appeal is a right given to the person in whose favour a Judge has decided. I think we ought not to enlarge that time, unless under some very special circumstances indeed …. One case was where there was anything like misleading on the part of the other side or some mistake in the office itself, where a man was misled by our own officer, or possibly some sudden accident which nothing could have foreseen—some sudden death, or something of that kind, which accounted for the delay, or cases like that. 54 That is still the law in England 138 years later: “the law exceptionally allows appeals out of time”. 55 It is also the current law in Alberta. 56 Third, Justice McGillivray favoured the view that misapprehension of the applicable rules by the applicant or counsel was not a valid ground—“a very special circumstance”—for an extension order. 57 Fourth, implementing the objective to secure the integrity of an order or judgment not appealed in time, Justice McGillivray held that it was “incumbent upon an applicant” to establish the six distinct conditions set out below: (1) “to show a bona fide intention to appeal held while the right to appeal existed” (2) “to account for the delay”; (3) “the failure to appeal was by reason of some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such a failure”; (4) “to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust having regard to the position of both parties to disturb the judgment”; (5) “to show that he had not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal”; (6) “to show that he had a reasonable chance of success if allowed to commence and prosecute the appeal”. 58 What does “incumbent” mean? 59 According to Webster's Third New International Dictionary, “incumbent”, as an adjective, means “falling or imposed as a duty, responsibility or obligation”. The Oxford English Dictionary presents a similar definition: “Resting or falling upon a person as a duty or obligation”. 60 One would have thought that, by using the word “incumbent” Justice McGillivray intended to impose an obligation on an applicant to satisfy the court that each of these six conditions existed before a time extension could be granted. The corollary of this principle is that an application will be denied if the applicant fails to establish one of the mandatory obligations. 61 This view is amply supported by Ramsdell v. Elliott, a judgment Justice McGillivray delivered six years later for a panel consisting of three of the five judges who heard Cairns v. Cairns. Justice McGillivray unequivocally affirmed that an applicant for an extension of time within which to appeal must establish all the conditions set out in Cairns v. Cairns: [C]ounsel for the respondent asked leave to appeal against … Ramsdell's judgment, notwithstanding that he was out of time in entering an appeal and notwithstanding that it is perfectly clear that the respondent had no intention of appealing while the right to appeal still existed. Mr. W. Kent Power, K.C., Editor-in-Chief of the Western Weekly Reports, has with his usual succinctness and accuracy summed up the judgment of this Court … in Cairns v. Cairns… as follows: Where a person has recovered a judgment and the time for giving notice of appeal therefrom has expired he has a vested interest in the judgment and in the benefits which may flow from it that will not be lightly interfered with by the Courts. Therefore an extension of time within which to give notice of appeal will not be granted as a matter of course, but a heavy burden rests on the applicant of showing cause why the indulgence of the Court should be extended to him. It is incumbent upon him: To show that a bona-fide intention to appeal was entertained while the right to appeal existed and that the failure to appeal was by reason of some special circumstance which served to excuse or justify such failure; To account for the delay and to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust, having regard to the position of both parties, to disturb the judgment; To show that he has not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal; To show that he would have a reasonable chance of success if allowed to prosecute the appeal. It introduced a level of predictability into the process and increased the likelihood that the appeal court would make consistent decisions. A rule that solely directs an adjudicator to do what justice requires introduces uncertainty, produces inconsistent and erratic jurisprudence, encourages groundless applications—no case is hopeless under such a regime—and inevitably drives up costs. 65 Regrettably, the final paragraphs of Justice McGillivray's Cairns opinion cast some doubt on the norm Justice McGillivray had formulated in the earlier portions of his opinion. In H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., 2024 ABKB 428, Justice Marion gave a summary of the law relating to the granting of extensions of the time period within which a third party notice must be filed and served. Justice Marion said: [17] Rule 3.45(c)(i) requires that third party claims must be filed and served on the plaintiff and the third party defendant within 6 months after the date on which the defendant filed a statement of defence or demand for notice. [18] The Court has the discretion to extend the time period under rule 3.45(c)(i) regardless of whether the time has expired: rule 13.5(2) and (3); Nelson & Nelson v Condominium Corporation No 0013187, 2019 ABQB 426 at para 49; Tole v Lucki, 2015 ABQB 231 at para 1; Condominium Plan 9812082 v Battistella Developments Inc, 2014 ABQB 644 at paras 9, 15 [Battistella]; Pagnucco v Sears Canada Inc, 2011 ABQB 810 at paras 9-11 (Master). [19] Over decades, dating back to at least the 1970s under previous iterations of Alberta’s Rules of Court, this Court has developed a framework to assess time extension applications for late third party notices in the exercise of the Court’s discretion. [20] The framework is reflected in numerous cases of our Court since the Rules were enacted in 2010. Although the specifics of the factors are sometimes described in different ways, the key factors are: (1) delay length; (2) the reason for the delay; and (3) prejudice: Kapeluck v Two Girls And A Hammer Inc, 2022 ABQB 467 at paras 3, 36; Piikani Nation v McMullen, 2020 ABQB 89 at para 29; Nelson at para 49; Stefanyk v Stevens, 2017 ABQB 402 at para 34; TRDMS Services Inc v Condo Corp 0425913 (the New Cambridge Lofts), 2016 ABQB 527 at paras 25-28; Battistella at para 15; Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman SA (Mittal Steel Roman SA), 2012 ABQB 679 at para 497 [Arcelormittal], var’d on other grounds 2013 ABCA 279, refused leave to appeal to SCC, 2014 CanLII 4542. [21] Each factor is considered concurrently rather than sequentially: Condominium Corporation No 9813678 v Statesman Corporation, 2008 ABQB 495 at para 45 [Statesman]; Dean v Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412 at para 66; Flight v Dillon, 2001 ABQB 211 at paras 26-28. [22] Although these three key factors are sometimes described as giving rise to a specific “test”, in my view they have never been described or intended to be exhaustive considerations. Courts will consider other factors which are either embedded within the key factors or as separate considerations. [23] For example, whether considered a distinct inquiry or part of the prejudice analysis, the Court will consider the merits of the proposed third party claim: Kapeluck at para 7; Stefanyk at para 34; Arcelormittal at para 500; TRDMS at paras 38-40; Bodnar Capital Corporation (301831 Alberta Ltd) v Synergy Projects Ltd, 2019 ABQB 528 at para 10 (Master); Condominium Corporation No 0425636 v Amyotte’s Plumbing Ltd, 2015 ABQB 801 at para 30 [Amyotte’s Plumbing]; Kwik-Kopy Printing Canada Corp v Skoreiko, 2002 ABQB 835 at para 37 (Master); Alliance Pipeline Limited Partnership v CE Franklin Ltd, 2007 ABQB 582 at para 12. [24] The merits threshold is low and has been described as only requiring that the claim have an “air of reality”, or a triable issue alleging facts that, if proved, would constitute a viable action: Arcelormittal at para 500; LaBell v Jo (R), 1990 ABCA 147 at para 4; Kapeluck at para 27; Van Troyen Holdings Ltd v Hunt Oil Company of Canada Inc, 2005 ABQB 626 at para 11; Primrose Drilling Ventures Ltd v Hitchner, 2005 ABQB 84 at para 28; Statesman at paras 46-49. [25] The Court will also consider the stage, status and pace of the underlying action, which can provide important context for the assessment of the key factors: Kapeluck at para 37; Battistella at paras 25-26; Nelson at para 57; Stefanyk at para 34; Arcelormittal at para 500; Spartek Systems Inc v Brown, 2009 ABQB 705 at para 14; Whitecourt Power Limited Partnership v Interpro Technical Services Ltd, 2014 ABQB 135 at para 15 (Master); Nova Pole International Inc v Trans America Group Ltd, 2010 ABQB 4 at para 41; Hein v Barrett, 2008 ABQB 548 at paras 17-23; Condominium Plan 9512180 v Prairie Land Corporation, 2008 ABQB 269 at para 29 [Prairie Land]; Van Troyen at para 13. For example, if the action has been moving slowly it may provide context for the reason for the delay and support an extension. If the litigation is in its early stages, there may be less prejudice to the proposed third party. On the other hand, if the litigation has been advancing quickly and the proposed third party has significant catch-up to do, or the matter is ready for trial, it may be evidence of prejudice. [26] The requirement to explain delay is mandatory; the onus is on the party moving for the time extension to lead evidence to explain the delay: Arcelormittal at para 498; Flight at para 11; Lister v Calgary (City), 1997 CanLII 24562 (AB CA) at para 14; ESM Transport Ltd v Western Mack Truck (Edmonton) Ltd, 1988 ABCA 157 at para 3. [27] Characterizing the delay length depends on the circumstances of the case. There is no magic formula or automatic result based on a specific delay length. Clearly, a longer delay weighs more against extending time than a shorter delay, and a shorter delay weighs more in favour of extending time. Courts have also recognized a relationship between delay length and the weight given to the other two key factors. When the delay is relatively short, more weight is given to the existence of prejudice resulting from the delay and, as the delay becomes longer, more weight is given to the reason, explanation or excuse for the delay: Nelson at para 51; Arcelormittal at para 499; Battistella at para 17; Piikani at para 38; TRMDS at para 37; Stefanyk at para 38; Amyotte’s Plumbing at para 20; Spartek at para 14; Flight at para 12. [28] For example, on one end of the spectrum, delays in the range of 10-14 months or less have been described as “relatively short”, “not unreasonable”, “not excessive”, “not substantial”, not long, or “not inordinate”: Arcelormittal at paras 499-519; Stefanyk at para 35; Alliance Pipeline at para 11; Lam v Bockman, 2006 ABQB 101; Amyotte’s Plumbing at paras 17-19; Prairie Land at para 30. In shorter delay cases, the explanation or excuse for the delay is less important to support an extension and the existence of prejudice is more important to resist it. If there is no prejudice, permission to file late is typically granted. [29] On the other end of the spectrum, delays over 50 months have consistently been considered inordinate, significant, or long: Piikani at para 30; Battistella at paras 16-17; Amoco Canada Petroleum Co Ltd v Propak Systems Ltd, 1999 ABQB 716 at paras 22-23. In these cases, proof of prejudice becomes less important, or may not even need to be materially considered if the delay cannot be justified, because prejudice may be “more or less” presumed, assumed or inferred: Battistella at para 26; Flight at para 13; Bow Valley Insurance Services (1992) Limited v Shah, 2005 ABCA 304 (also known as Calgary Mack Sales Ltd v Shah) at para 24, leave to appeal to SCC refused; Dean at para 66. Leave will generally be denied where there is delay of this nature and there is no or insufficient evidence to reasonably explain or excuse it: Arcelormittal at para 499. [30] Many cases fall between these two extremes. They can be more difficult to assess, requiring a more nuanced balancing between the relative strength and weight of the key factors in all the circumstances of the case. 4. Review of Accounts—Extension of Time In Lewis Estates Communities Inc. v. Brownlee LLP, 2013 ABQB 508, 2013 CarswellAlta 1704, clients filed Appointments for Taxation (the term used under the previous Rules) prior to the new Rules being adopted. Mr. Justice Brown concluded that “while the Appointments are governed by the Old Rules, the application to extend the time period for seeking a review of Brownlee's accounts is governed by the Rule 13.5(2)(a) of the Rules of Court”[his Lordship referred to Samson Cree Nation v. O'Reilly & Associés, 2013 ABQB 350, 2013 CarswellAlta 1065, 564 A.R. 169, 46 C.P.C. (7th) 341 at paragraph 156]. His Lordship said, at paragraphs 29–39: 29 While, therefore, the six month rule can be circumvented by an exercise of my discretion to extend the review period beyond six months, I must bear in mind that it exists for good reasons. Where I choose to exercise my discretion to extend the time period beyond six months, I must do so judicially and in the interests of justice. This means I must weigh the factors relevant in the circumstances of this application to the exercise of my discretion, having regard to established principles and to whether exercising (or not exercising) my discretion would produce injustice or unfairness. (Mitrovic v. Mitrovic, 2007 ABQB 107 at para. 7, Veit J). 30 This Court has on several prior occasions articulated an array of factors to be considered on an application to extend the time period for a review of lawyers' charges, some of which might have more case-specific application than others. There is, however, no preordained checklist of factors to be reviewed in each case. Nor should there be. The exercise (or non-exercise) of my discretion must be informed by considerations that apply to this particular application. 31 Prior decisions of this court have adopted a similarly case-specific approach to the factors to be considered. In Poundmakers Lodge v. Scott & Co, 2002 ABQB 745 (at para 13), Read J, having reviewed the jurisprudence and the circumstances of that application, considered the following four factors: 1. Did the delay in filing the taxation cause prejudice to the solicitor? 2. When did the client express the intent to tax the accounts? 3. Were the accounts part of a continuing file and therefore interim accounts? 4. Is there evidence that there was an overcharging and that it is just and equitable that the accounts be taxed? 32 In Prophet River First Nation v. Rath & Company, 2011 ABQB 408 at para. 21, Macleod J also thought it important to answer these questions: 1. Is there evidence that the parties have come to an agreement as to the amount of the account? 2. Does the evidence of the entire relationship between the solicitor and client support any extension of time? 33 To the six factors considered in Poundmakers Lodge and in Prophet River, taken together, Rooke ACJ added another factor in Samson Cree (at para. 39), which is whether the applicant has a reasonable excuse for failing to seek a review within six months. He relied upon the decision of Master Laycock in BA Capital Inc. v. Focussed Money Solutions Inc., 2012 ABQB 379, which stated (at paras. 8-9): In this application the first consideration is whether or not the applicants can satisfy me that they have a reasonable excuse for failing to bring the disputed accounts before a Review Officer within six months of the bill being delivered. In the case of a series of interim accounts, it is the date of the delivery of the final bill that is material. See Baxandall v. Peterson Hustwick Wetsch & Moffat (1994), 154 A.R. 353 (Q.B.). In this case the applicant has provided no evidence in his affidavit to explain the 16 month delay following the final account in bringing this application or when he became concerned about the size of the account or the performance of the law firm. 34 Most recently, Burrows J, in Thistle v. Stringam Denecky LLP, 2013 ABQB 372, after acknowledging Poundmakers Lodge, Prophet River and BA Capital Inc., rejected Master Laycock's analysis in BA Capital, which appeared to have held that the failure to account for a delay beyond six months is fatal to the application for an extension of time. Burrows J said, and I agree, that the quality of an explanation, or its absence, is only one factor to be taken into account. He added (at para. 19) that “[i]n a case such as this, where the delay has been short, the absence of an explanation is of much less significance than the absence of evidence of prejudice.” (The final account in that case had been sent eight months prior to the client seeking a review). 35 In addition to several of the factors listed above, Burrows J also considered, first, whether there “appears to be possible merit to the client's position that the accounts were excessive”. While he cautioned that it is not his role to consider the actual merits, he viewed it as relevant to the exercise of his discretion to consider whether the client's complaint appears to have sufficient merit to justify a review. This makes sense. There is no point to this Court exercising its discretion to further an obviously hopeless cause. Secondly, Burrows J considered whether the extension request was for a significant period of time, stating (at paras. 29-30): Where a client seeks to have an account reviewed many months after it was rendered the application should be viewed differently than where the required extension is small. The smaller the sought extension, the easier it should be to obtain it. This is undoubtedly related to the prejudice point previously discussed. Prejudice to the firm's ability to defend the accounts at the review is likely to be minimal if the delay is short. Here the sought extension is 2 months. That is short. 36 The various factors identified in prior decisions of this Court are not watertight compartments. (For example, Read J's factor of when the intent to tax first expressed overlaps with Master Laycock's and Rooke ACJ's factor of the reason for the delay. Her factor of possible overcharging also overlaps with Burrows J's consideration of whether the applicant's case appears to have “possible merit”. And, as will be seen, Burrows J's consideration of length of time of the extension overlaps somewhat with the consideration of prejudice to the lawyer.) Moreover, some of the factors may not apply in every case. (For example, the factor of whether the parties have come to an agreement as to the amount of the account would not work in favour of or against either the Applicants or Brownlee.) All this means is that the considerations to be applied here are to be examined (as they were in Samson Cree and Prophet River) in relation to each other. 37 Taking all of the foregoing into account as well as the circumstances of this particular matter, I view the following considerations as having the most significance to deciding this application: 1. Accounts: What sort of accounts did Brownlee render to the Applicants? 2. Length of Time of Extension: Is the extension sought for a short or long period of time? 3. Reason for Delay: Why did the Applicants fail to file their Appointments prior to the expiration of 6 months? 4. Prejudice: Did the delay in filing the Appointments cause prejudice to Brownlee? 5. Evidence of Overcharging: Is there evidence that (absent a satisfactory answer from Brownlee) might merit a finding of overcharging, such that it is just that the accounts be reviewed? 6. Relationship: Does the evidence of the entire relationship between Brownlee and the Applicants support an extension of time? 38 No single factor is, on its own, determinative. For example, the absence of prejudice in and of itself would be insufficient to permit the Applicants to obtain a review of Brownlee's accounts. (Poundmakers Lodge, at para. 18.) 39 While there is no particular order in which most of these factors should be considered, the type of accounts rendered by Brownlee is pivotal to some of the other factors (in particular the length of time extension and the reason for the delay), and so I will consider that first. His Lordship then discussed each of the four considerations. He said: (1)—Accounts 41 In Samson Cree (at paras. 18–43), Rooke ACJ clarified the different types of retainers that govern the lawyer-client relationship. I will not review all of them here. The issue to decide here is whether Brownlee's periodic accounts (being accounts that were sent out at intervals during the term of the retainer) were interim or final. On this distinction, Rooke ACJ said (at paras. 45–46): Periodic accounts may be interim or final. An interim account is one that is not final, but is issued pending a final account, and may be changed directly at any future time or in the end result between the time it is issued and the final account. It is thus customary that interim accounts are not the subject of taxation individually, but rather only the final account. When the final account is taxed, all the interim accounts issued leading to the final account are taxable. Final accounts are ones that conclude all truly interim or provisional accounts before them (in which case, as noted, all the interim accounts are part of that taxation), or are final and taxable in themselves, with no regard to other accounts. 42 As to determining whether a periodic account is interim or final, Rooke ACJ undertook a comprehensive review of the authorities (including Sharma; Raithby v. Fraser & Beatty (2000), 47 OR (3d) 245 (SCJ); Enterprise Rent-a-Car Co v. Shapiro, Cohen, Andrews, Findlayson (1998), 38 OR (3d) 257 (CA); Siegel v. Cameron & Cameron, [1996] A.J. No. 757 (QB); Nathanson, Schachter & Thompson v. Levitt, 2004 BCSC 1402; Poundmakers Lodge; Morin, Grant v. Olsson (1994), 37 CPC (3d) 130 (BCSC); Siegel v. Cameron & Cameron, [1996] A.J. No. 757 (QB); Robertson, Ward, Suderman & Bowes v. BC (BC Transit), (1987) 19 BCLR (2d) 1, [1988] 1 WWR 649 (CA); and Re Romer & Haslam, [1893] 2 QB 286 (CA)). Taken together, these authorities have focussed on whether the lawyer and the client considered each of the accounts in question to be the lawyer's final account for the work recorded. And, in determining with regard to the dealings of the parties and the circumstances whether the parties intended that each account would be final, they establish that a periodic account is likely to be considered final when the where the parties understand that the lawyer's charges will be based upon hours spent and the lawyers' billable rates, and that the charges will not be adjusted, whether upwards or downwards, upon issuance of a final bill at the conclusion of the matter. … (2)—Length of Time of Extension 47 While the fact that each of Brownlee's accounts was a final account does not weigh against granting any extension of time, it does mean Rule 647's six month time period runs separately from the time each separate account was sent. Consequently, the length of the necessary extension of time varies with each account …. (3)—Reason for Delay 48 There ought to be a very good reason supporting any extension of time for seeking a review of lawyers' charges, consistent with the values which underlie the six month rule. Is there some explanation as to why, in six months, the Applicants could not have formed and stated their concerns. … (4)—Prejudice … 64 In short, a rebuttable presumption of prejudice arises in the face of inordinate delay. Two issues arise from this: first, whether the Applicants' delay was inordinate; and, second, whether they have rebutted the presumed prejudice to Brownlee. 65 In Samson Cree (at para. 201), Rooke ACJ held that, generally, a review of lawyers' charges initiated within the two year limitation period is not prejudicial. This necessarily means that, in Rooke ACJ's view, a delay of less than two years is not inordinate. The Associate Chief Justice relied upon the decision of Slatter J (as he then was) in Sharma, where he said (at para. 36): The purpose of a statute of limitations is to prevent the prosecution of stale claims. The principle is that persons with claims should not sleep on them, and if they do sleep on them then the claims will be barred. Potential defendants are entitled to know that, after a certain period of time, dated claims will not be pursued against them, and they can conduct their affairs accordingly: …James H. Meek, Jr. Trust v. San Juan Resources Inc.., [2005] A.J. No. 1754, 2005 ABCA 448 at para. 37. Once a client is served with an Appointment for Taxation, the client knows that the lawyer is seeking payment. The Appointment starts a chain of events leading to a remedial order. Taxation is a “civil procedure”. As long as the Appointment is issued within two years of the original debt, then the claim is not seen as being stale by the law of limitations. The mere fact that the enforcement proceedings are started by an Appointment for Taxation, as opposed to a Statement of Claim, should not make any difference. The lawyer has commenced enforcement of the claim within the period provided for by the limitations statute, and the client is aware within that period that the claim is being advanced. The purposes of the Limitations Act are met. There is nothing in the wording of the Act to require a proceeding commenced by a more formal or traditional process. 66 With great respect to Rooke ACJ, I do not take this passage from Slatter J's reasons as speaking of prejudice, but rather of whether the taking out of a Notice for Appointment of Taxation is a remedial order within the meaning of the Limitations Act, and is therefore subject to the two year statutory limitation period. 67 If I am wrong about that, I nonetheless find myself in respectful disagreement with the general statement in Samson Cree that a review of lawyers' charges initiated within the two year limitation period is not prejudicial. It must be remembered that the Limitations Act already precludes a review of lawyers' charges incurred more than two years prior to the client seeking a review. (Sharma, at paras. 33–36). If, therefore, prejudice is a factor to be considered on an application to extend the time for reviewing a lawyer's charges (and Poundmakers Lodge, Prophet River and Samson Cree state that it is), then it must contemplate that such prejudice will always arise within the two year statutory limitation period. Otherwise, any consideration of prejudice would be otiose. … (5)—Evidence of Overcharging 72 This factor, which as mentioned was emphasized by Burrows J in Thistle, requires me to consider whether there is evidence that might merit a finding of overcharging, such that it is just that the accounts be reviewed. The Applicants emphasize, in keeping with Burrows J's direction in Thistle (at para. 26), that they are not seeking from me a determination of whether Brownlee's accounts are reasonable or not, but the opportunity to have a review officer make that determination. … 75 Re Thompson's[Re Thompson (1867), 2 Chy Chmbrs 100] threshold of “gross overcharge” does not bind me, nor do I take it as stating the law of Alberta. The central question for the purpose of considering this factor is not how much a client may or may not have been overcharged, but whether there is evidence that might merit a finding of overcharging. I agree with Brownlee, however, that this process (of the Applicants seeking an extension of time) entitles Brownlee to remain silent without fear of an adverse inference as to the merits of the complaint about overcharging. That silence, however, requires the Court to apply this factor without the benefit of Brownlee's explanation. … (6)—Relationship 76 Does the evidence of the entire relationship between Brownlee and the Applicants support an extension of time? 77 As a starting point, I must bear in mind that the relationship under consideration here is the lawyer-client relationship. As such, it presupposes that some degree of trust is reposed in the lawyer (although the degree will differ among lawyer-client relationships. See Galambos v. Perez, 2009 SCC 48 at para. 38). Indeed, that trust is why clients such as the Applicants retain lawyers. (Adams v. Law Society of Alberta, 2000 ABCA 240 at para. 10.) 78 Rule 647(d) of the Old Rules, and its successor Rules 10.10(2) and 13.5(2)(a) of the Rules of Court, therefore presuppose that the relationship between the parties is characterized by the client's trust in the lawyer's qualities, including his or her integrity. This characteristic must inform any analysis under these particular rules; that is, the relationship is inherently built upon the client's trust in the lawyer's integrity. At the same time, because this characteristic is inherent (albeit to differing degrees) in every lawyer-client relationship, I must in weighing this factor also look to the qualities of this particular lawyer-client relationship. 5. Special Circumstances In Cairns v. Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R. 335, 26 Alta. L.R. 69, McGillivray J.A. after setting out the above rules considered several conflicting English decisions. He quoted from a judgment of Brett M.R. who had stated in Re Manchester Economic Building Society (1883), 24 Ch. D. 488 at 497: I know of no other rule than this, that the Court has power to give the special leave, and exercising its judicial discretion is bound to give the special leave, if justice requires that that leave should be given. The cases which were brought before the Court were cases in which either justice did require that the leave should be given or justice required that it should not be given. McGillivray J.A. then continued at p. 346: I think that the view of Brett, M.R. is to be preferred to that of James, L.J. but whatever may be said as to the conflicting decisions under the special language of the English Rule I think that it can be laid down that under our Rules this Court considers that it has a free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case. This division has relieved an applicant from its failure to comply with any of the four matters noted if there are special circumstances entitling the applicant to relief. To simply lay down that the court will extend the time to appeal when the justice of the situation so requires gives little help to members of the bar in deciding how to advise a client. This division considers it more advantageous to require an applicant to direct his attention to the four matters specified than to lay down as a general rule that time will be extended when the justice of the situation requires. Royal Bank v. Morin (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 127at 129 (C.A.). In Stoddard v. Montague (2006), 412 A.R. 88 (Alta. C.A.), the Court re-affirmed the above position, and said, at p. 91: Generally, the applicant must meet all four criteria. However, if there are “unique and special circumstances” and it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court may “excuse compliance with one or more of the criteria” and exercise its discretion to grant the extension in any event.… 6. “Prejudice” Must Relate to Extension Sought We are all of the view that this appeal must be dismissed. Counsel for Mr. Grotski has referred us to the decisions of this court in Cairns v. Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R. 335, and Royal Bank of Canada v. Morin and Twelsey et al. (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 127. These cases, and in particular Cairns v. Cairns, set out the relevant considerations on an application to extend the time for appeal. In relation to them counsel argues that Mr. Grotski has suffered prejudice in that the limitation period for the commencement of this action expired in 1987, three years after the action was commenced and more than three years before the order which the bank seeks to appeal. In our view this prejudice is no greater than that suffered by any party where an extension of time to appeal is granted to the opposing party. It is not prejudice which arises from the very short delay which resulted when the notice of appeal filed by the bank was filed in the wrong action. Bank of Montreal v. Grotski (1992), 120 A.R. 149 (C.A.) at 150. 7. Evidence in Support of Application Where a party seeks a significant time extension, it is expected to give evidence to explain the delay, i.e. why prompt compliance did not occur. Maybe it would be different if the extension sought was slight, but here the delay was over four and one-half years. Evidence must be proper admissible evidence such as an affidavit, not mere allegations by counsel. The cases on time extensions generally, and those on later third party notices, seem to agree on those points. Lister v. Calgary (City) (1997), 47 Alta. L.R. (3d) 14 (C.A.), at 16, per curiam. 8. Rule 13.5 Does Not Extend Statutory Time Limits That leaves the problem of time. Section 152(2) of the Planning Act requires that “an application for leave … shall be made … within 30 days after the issue of the order, decision, permit or approval sought to be appealed”. That being a statutory time limit, it is trite law that the court cannot extend it, and rule 548 on extending time limits does not apply. Houg Alberta Ltd. v. 417034 Alberta Ltd. (1991), 117 A.R. 196 at 200 (C.A.). In Lakevold v. Dome Petroleum Ltd. (1979), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1, the Court of Appeal again considered the matter of using R. 548 to extend statutory time limits. At p. 3 Lieberman J.A., speaking for the court, said: We have considered the case of Duzs v. Duzs, [1973] 3 W.W.R. 394, a judgment of this Division, dealing with restrictions with respect to time found in the Divorce Act. Allen, J.A. considers Rule 458 and at pp. 397-398 says this: Rule 548 of the Rules of Court dealing with the power of the Court to enlarge or abridge time fixed for doing any act reads as follows: . . . . . It has been held however that such a Rule does not apply where the time for appealing is fixed by statute which confers no power on the court to extend time: see Re Fair and Toronto, 65 O.L.R. 176 at 179 (C.A.), per Masten J.A.; and Re MacDonald, 23 Sask. L.R. 327 (C.A.), per Haultain C.J.S. I believe the principle laid down in these cases has been adopted and followed in our Court, although I am unable to find a report of an Alberta case directly in point. In the context of the Duzs case the above comments are dicta. We respectfully adopt this dicta as an accurate statement of the law and would apply it to the facts of this case. In Black Diamond Land & Cattle Co. v. Oasis Gardeners Ltd. (1996), 189 A.R. 318 (Q.B.), Sulatycky J. (as he then was), said at p. 320: “A court cannot alter or extend statutory deadlines unless there is express statutory permission to do so”. However, in Walker v. Canadian Tire Corp. (1992), 128 A.R. 229 (Q.B.), O'Leary J. held that the procedural (not substantive) statutory time limit for filing a transcript as required in an appeal from Provincial Court—Civil Division to the Court of Queen's Bench could be extended under R. 548. His Lordship said at pp. 232–33: In my view, Yorkshire Trust and other cases which hold that the court cannot extend time limits imposed by statute under rule 548 or its inherent power (see Stevenson & Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, at p. 1000) have no application here where the time limit is not substantive but procedural. In my view this court has authority, under either rule 548 or its inherent power to control its own process, to enlarge the six-month period fixed by s. 59(3) on application made before or after expiration of the time. It is significant that s. 59(2) permits the Court of Queen's Bench, on application made “before or after the expiration of the periods fixed by subsection (1)(a) and (b)”, to extend the times within which the steps referred to in those clauses may be done. It would be anomalous to construe subs. (3) as permitting an extension of time only if application is made prior to its expiration. The intention to create such an unreasonable situation cannot be attributed to the legislature. Section 61(1) of the Act says that if an appellant fails to comply with the requirements of s. 59, “the appeal shall be dismissed”. If any failure to comply with s. 59 compels dismissal, as subs. (1) seems to say, the power to enlarge time given by subs. (2) and (3) would be of no effect. In the context of the Act, the word “shall” in s. 61(1) cannot be construed as mandatory without totally depriving s. 59(2) and (3) of significance. It must be interpreted as permissive and, so viewed, does not exclude operation of the inherent power of the court to extend the time for completing a procedural step. Lastly on this point, I refer to s. 75 of the Act: No proceeding is invalid for informality if there has been substantial compliance with the requirements of this Part. This indicates that the provisions of the Act dealing with matters of form, as opposed to substance, are to be construed liberally. To the extent that the words in question will bear such a meaning they are to be given a meaning which recognizes that litigants in the Civil Division and before this court on appeal are not usually represented by lawyers. The object of the portion of the Act which deals with civil claims is to provide a simple and easily understood procedure for asserting and defending claims and appealing decisions of the Civil Division. If the words of s. 59(3) and s. 61(1) were interpreted literally, they would present a trap for the unwary. I am satisfied that the construction I have placed upon them is in accordance with the intention of the legislature and the objects of the Act. The strength of the appeal is irrelevant on a motion to extend time. But in ordinary appeals, the right to extend time arises only through the general time extension rule, R. 548 … On motions for security or a stay, the strength of the appeal may be relevant. But on a motion to extend time, strength is irrelevant unless the appeal is virtually hopeless. Levesque v. Levesque (1992), 3 Alta. L.R. (3d) 193 (C.A.), at 196, 197, per Côté J.A.

The relevant portion of the [W.W.R.] headnote reads: Where a person has recovered a judgment and the time for giving notice of appeal therefrom has expired he has a vested interest in the judgment and in the benefits which may flow from it that will not lightly be interfered with by the Courts.

Therefore an extension of time within which to give notice of appeal will not be granted as a matter of course, but a heavy burden rests on the applicant of showing cause why the indulgence of the court should be extended to him.
It is incumbent upon him:

(1) To show that a bona-fide intention to appeal was entertained while the right to appeal existed and that the failure to appeal was by reason of some special circumstance which served to excuse or justify such failure
(2) To account for the delay and to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust, having regard to the position of both parties, to disturb the judgment
(3) To show that he has not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal
(4) To show that he would have a reasonable chance of success if allowed to prosecute the appeal.

Cairns, a 1931 judgment, and Ramsdell v.

Elliott, a 1936 opinion, the Alberta Supreme Court Appellate Division laid the foundation for the test to be applied when assessing the merits of an application to extend the time for filing a notice of appeal.

They recognize that an unappealed judgment or order is a valuable asset for the victorious party that should not be devalued “unless weighty reasons be given for asking the Court to interfere with that right”.
The importance placed on the principle of finality prompted the Court to place a “heavy burden [on the applicant]… of showing cause why the indulgence of the Court should be granted”.
The two judgments identified and confirmed six conditions that an applicant seeking leave to file a late notice of appeal must meet to secure the requested relief.
6 First, did the applicant form an intention to appeal while the right of appeal existed?
7 Second, has the applicant provided an explanation for the failure to file a timely appeal?
8 Third, if so, does this explanation constitute “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such failure”?
9 Fourth, has the applicant demonstrated that the delay has not “so seriously prejudiced [the respondent] as to make it unjust” to grant a time extension?
10 Fifth, has the applicant not taken the benefits of the judgment?
11 Sixth, it falls on the applicant to convince the court that “he had a reasonable chance of success if allowed to commence and prosecute the appeal”.
12 Stoddard v.
Montague, a 2006 judgment, modified the old standard.
The new formulation recognized that an applicant who demonstrated compliance with all six criteria was “generally” entitled to an extension.
But now an applicant who missed one or more of the markers could still prevail “if there are ‘unique and special circumstances’ and it is in the interests of justice to [grant the extension]”.

49 It merits careful study.
50 Justice McGillivray wrote for a five-member panel.
His judgment stands for four propositions.

51 First, a judgment that has not been appealed within the stipulated time frame is a valuable asset to the victorious party.24 “When the time for appealing has expired, the litigation is at an end; the successful party is entitled to the benefit of the judgment in his or her favour.
At that stage, the successful party has a ‘vested right to retain the judgment’.” 52 Second, an unappealed decision is a final decision.
Finality is so important that it ought to be disturbed only in extraordinary circumstances.

Justice McGillivray held that “the holder of a judgment after the time for giving notice of appeal has expired, has a special right or interest which will not be set aside by the Courts, unless weighty reasons be given for asking the Court to interfere with that right”.
53 Lord Justice James, in International Financial Society (Ltd.) v.

City of Moscow Gas Co., an 1878 judgment that Justice McGillivray cited, made it very clear that an extension would seldom be granted: The limitation of the time to appeal is a right given to the person in whose favour a Judge has decided.
I think we ought not to enlarge that time, unless under some very special circumstances indeed ….

One case was where there was anything like misleading on the part of the other side or some mistake in the office itself, where a man was misled by our own officer, or possibly some sudden accident which nothing could have foreseen—some sudden death, or something of that kind, which accounted for the delay, or cases like that.
54 That is still the law in England 138 years later: “the law exceptionally allows appeals out of time”.
55 It is also the current law in Alberta.
56 Third, Justice McGillivray favoured the view that misapprehension of the applicable rules by the applicant or counsel was not a valid ground—“a very special circumstance”—for an extension order.

57 Fourth, implementing the objective to secure the integrity of an order or judgment not appealed in time, Justice McGillivray held that it was “incumbent upon an applicant” to establish the six distinct conditions set out below:
(1) “to show a bona fide intention to appeal held while the right to appeal existed”
(2) “to account for the delay”
(3) “the failure to appeal was by reason of some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such a failure”
(4) “to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust having regard to the position of both parties to disturb the judgment”
(5) “to show that he had not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal”
(6) “to show that he had a reasonable chance of success if allowed to commence and prosecute the appeal”.
58 What does “incumbent” mean?
59 According to Webster's Third New International Dictionary, “incumbent”, as an adjective, means “falling or imposed as a duty, responsibility or obligation”.
The Oxford English Dictionary presents a similar definition: “Resting or falling upon a person as a duty or obligation”.

64 In providing a concise codification of the case law, Justice McGillivray provided a great service to the legal community.
His Cairns v.

Cairns test introduced a workable standard that enabled skilled counsel to provide sound advice to clients about the status of an unappealed order or judgment and ensured that judges had an analytical framework to apply when hearing time-extension applications.
It introduced a level of predictability into the process and increased the likelihood that the appeal court would make consistent decisions.

A rule that solely directs an adjudicator to do what justice requires introduces uncertainty, produces inconsistent and erratic jurisprudence, encourages groundless applications—no case is hopeless under such a regime—and inevitably drives up costs.
65 Regrettably, the final paragraphs of Justice McGillivray's Cairns opinion cast some doubt on the norm Justice McGillivray had formulated in the earlier portions of his opinion.

In the context of considering whether the applicant should be allowed to file a second application for a time extension “to meet the requirements mentioned”, the judge said this: [T]his Court considers that it has a free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case. … This does not mean that this Court will exercise its discretion loosely. … In the application of this rule due regard will be had to the successful litigant's vested interest in his judgment, and so the Court will scrutinize with care the material offered in support of a claim to have that interest set aside if it establishes those things that I have indicated it is incumbent upon the applicant to prove but once satisfied as to this the Court will grant or refuse the extension of time as the interests of judgment seem to require.
66 These paragraphs admittedly add a level of uncertainty to the judgment.
Two different concepts derive some support from these concluding passages.
67 First, even if the applicant satisfies the adjudicator that the six Cairns criteria have been met, there is a residual discretion to deny the application.
This is not an unsound refinement.

Suppose that there is a dispute about the mother's entitlement, over the objection of the children's father, to leave Alberta with the couple's six and seven-year-old children, so that she can remarry and start a new life in Montreal.
The chambers judge allows her to go to Montreal with the children.
The self-represented father does not appeal in time.
He suffers a concussion before the appeal deadline expires and is ill for months.
It is conceivable that a court, mindful of the best interests of the children, would be extremely reluctant to introduce uncertainty into the family dynamics.
The youngsters have started school, settled in with their new blended family and made new friends.
68 Second, even if an applicant fails to convince the adjudicator that all the criteria have been established, the court may still grant the application.
This is not an implausible interpretation, given the statement that the court “has free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done”.

It may be desirable to extend the appeal period by a matter of days to cover the exigencies associated with the practice of law without the necessity of expending much of the parties' time and money and the resources of the court.
