He provided this gloss: “if the applicant does satisfy all the components of the Cairns test, it is highly likely that an extension will be granted”.
I agree.
There is a presumption that an applicant who complies with all the Cairns elements and applies for relief immediately is entitled to an extension.
There may be extraordinary circumstances that cause a court to deny an application that should presumptively be granted.
The family law mobility example that I gave earlier comes to mind.
98 My colleague also varied somewhat the answer to the second query that I understand Stoddard v.
Montague provided—what is the best way to respond to an applicant who does not convince the adjudicator that he or she has fully satisfied the six-part test?

Instead of insisting that the applicant who falls short present “unique and special circumstances and [show that] it is in the interests of justice to do so”, the chambers judge adopted a less onerous standard: “Since there is an overriding discretion in the Court to extend the time to appeal, it is not necessary for an applicant to satisfy all components of the Cairns test …[I]n the end the Cairns factors and the surrounding circumstances must be considered and weighed collectively in deciding whether an extension of time is warranted”.
To my mind, the need for “unique and special circumstances” and a demonstration that an extension is “in the interests of justice” is an important aspect of the test adopted by Stoddard v.
Montague that should not be abandoned.
The facts in Smoky Lake General & Auxiliary Hospital & Nursing Home District v.
Higdon come to mind.
Even though the applicant did not originally intend to appeal, it was dissatisfied with the judgment and promptly took other steps to deprive the order to which it objected of legal effect.
If the time to appeal was not extended, it is arguable that an intolerable legal result would follow—there would be two inconsistent orders.
99 The chambers judge in Attila Dogan Construction made one other alteration to the Cairns criteria.

He jettisoned the second criteria—“the failure to appeal was by reason of some very special circumstance” and adopted a much less demanding norm—“some acceptable explanation for the lateness”: It is true that Cairns contemplates “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify” the late appeal.
Cairns, however, was a custody dispute engaging the interests of a child: finality was of prime importance, and the procedural history was unsatisfactory.
While some acceptable explanation for the lateness is required, the reason, considered in isolation, need not be “very special”.
100 I would not revise this element.
It is an essential component of the Cairns v.
Cairns test.
101 Several reasons account for this opposition.
102 First, Justice McGillivray formulated the test for all classes of cases, not just custody disputes, which was the issue before the Cairns court.

One must remember that Justice McGillivray worked with a specific framework—an unappealed judgment or order is a valuable right and the applicant who seeks an indulgence has a “heavy burden” to discharge.
103 Second, while rule compliance was an important goal in 1931 when Justice McGillivray delivered the Cairns v.
Cairns judgment, rule compliance has become an even more important objective after October 31, 2010, the date the new Alberta Rules of Court came into force.

The amount of time and money it takes to resolve disputes has expanded exponentially, the percentage of cases resolved by trial has contracted considerably since 193182 and a new set of values governing litigation is in place.
Lawyers have an obligation to proceed with reasonable dispatch and courts understand the need to expedite and finalize disputes and to promote rule compliance.

104 Rule 1.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court declares that “[t]he purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and cost-effective way”.
This theme is repeated in s.
1.2(3)(a), a provision that obliges a litigant to “facilitate the quickest means of resolving the claim at the least expense”.

105 Justice is more than a defensible and rational explanation for the disposition a court pronounces that explains to the parties and the community why the dispute was resolved the way it was; it is also a predisposition to the insistence that disputes be resolved as quickly as reasonably possible in accordance with the time lines fashioned by procedural rules. “Expedition in dispute resolution and finality of litigation are not in competition with justice, but on the contrary are dictated by the considerations of justice.” Delay is not an attribute of justice.
106 This means that the six criteria Justice McGillivray formulated must not be diluted and the bar lowered.
Such a reading would frustrate one of the overarching objectives of the Alberta Rules of Court—timely resolution of disputes.
The bar must be high and difficult to clear.
This Court must send an unequivocal message that time limits are of fundamental importance and must be observed, except in extraordinary circumstances.

107 If this Court insists on strict rule compliance and forgives noncompliance only in extraordinary circumstances there will be a reduction in the number of missed appeal deadlines and less of this court's time will be devoted to hearing time extension applications, a nonproductive use of judicial resources.
I am convinced that there is a direct correlation between the approach courts take to rule compliance and the prevalence of rule compliance in litigation.
Litigants who know that the courts will insist on adherence to timelines are much more likely to abide by the rules.

Those responsible for the manner in which lawyers discharge their duties to their clients—law societies—and lawyers' insurers will devote more resources to reducing the risk that barristers will breach the time periods embedded in the civil procedure rules. … 116 This Court has historically favoured a regime that places an onerous burden on those who wish to use the secondary appeal window.
A desire to promote rule-compliance probably accounts for the standards Justice McGillivray favoured in Cairns v.
Cairns and Ramsdell v.
Elliott.
The same is true today.
Our Court still recognizes the fundamental importance of Cairns v.

Cairns, the primacy of the finality principle and appreciates that the objectives of the Alberta Rules of Court will be unattainable if rule compliance is abandoned as a critical attribute of a modern justice system.
117 This philosophy has produced a norm that has three features.
118 First, the obligation in r.
14.8(2)(iii) of the Alberta Rules of Court—file and serve a notice of appeal within a month after the date of decision—is much more important than r.
13.5(2)(a)—the provision that allows the court to extend a time period.
This Court must strictly enforce time lines to ensure that disputes are resolved in a timely way and to give credence to the principles of finality.
119 The first feature leads directly to the second.
120 Second, a decision that has not been appealed within the stipulated period allowed for an appeal is a valuable asset for the party who prevailed.
This interest should be compromised only in exceptional circumstances.
121 Third, the court's jurisdiction to reopen the window for filing an appeal should be exercised in two different types of exceptional circumstances.
122 The first category or set captures applicants who request an indulgence measured in a small number of days.
123 It consists of two subsets.
124 The first subset is populated by applicants who have complied with the Cairns v.
Cairns standard, triggering the presumption noted above, and acted as quickly as possible to file a time-extension application.

In addition, an applicant who, while the primary appeal window was still open, notified the respondent in unequivocal terms that an appeal would be filed has increased the likelihood that the court will respond positively to an extension application.

The short period of additional time and the advance notice diminishes the importance of the respondent's expectation interest that with the passage of the appeal period without an appeal the order to which the applicant objects is immune from review.
A respondent having received notice of the applicant's intention to appeal before the appeal period closed would have no sound basis on which to object to a slight delay.
This exception will account for a large number of successful applications.
125 The second subset captures the situation where the applicant does not meet all of the Cairns v.
Cairns milestones and does not activate the presumption.
But the applicant still moves with alacrity to remedy the deficiency and has an appeal that meets the merits-based component of the Cairns v.
Cairns milestones.
It makes no sense to extend the time for filing by even a day if it is patent that the applicant has a frivolous appeal.
A fact pattern that features facts comparable to those presented by Smoky Lake General & Auxiliary Hospital & Nursing Home District No.
Higdon may be classified as a subset two case.
Suppose that the applicant was dissatisfied with a decision but instead of appealing, pursued other remedies.
By the time that the applicant appreciated that its initial response was unwise and that an appeal was the best option, the appeal period had elapsed.
The applicant promptly applies for relief.

126 The second category or set of exceptional circumstances collects those extraordinary scenarios that result in an applicant seeking an extension that is for a considerable period of time—well in excess of several days.

This set consists of cases where it would be unjust not to accommodate the applicant's request for additional time notwithstanding the passage of several weeks or more after the appeal deadline expired.
127 This may be the case if the applicant or counsel or both encounter events over which the applicant and counsel had no control, such as a natural disaster.

Suppose that a lawyer's office is flooded or destroyed by a forest fire and it takes some time for the practitioner to reestablish normal routines and discharge commitments to clients and other lawyers.
Or suppose that a lawyer or client or both are incapacitated by illness or injury and are unable to manage their affairs.
This may happen if a sole practitioner is involved in an automobile accident and is in a coma.
Or a lawyer may experience mental health problems that prevent him or her from making the decisions needed to protect the clients' interests.

Because the applicant bears the burden to prove the facts that serve as the basis for the exercise of the court's discretion in the applicant's favour the applicant must provide expert evidence to substantiate any claim of incapacitation.

It is also conceivable that a court may also react positively if any delay is attributable to the failure of counsel to protect the applicant's interests and an action against the lawyer for damages arising from the lawyer's negligence would not provide an adequate remedy.
Suppose that a lawyer's misconduct jeopardized the future right of the applicant to occupy property that he had improved and resided on most of his life.
128 But the delay that may be sanctioned for this second category of exceptional cases is not indefinite in nature.

There comes a point—perhaps in the two to three month range—when the values the finality principle protects and the need to validate the reasonable expectations of the successful party far exceeds that associated with any interest the applicant may have in securing the judgment of an appeal court on the merits of the decision to which the applicant objects.
At this point, the court should not exercise its discretion in favour of the applicant. … 181 Mr.
Travis' former counsel knew what had to be done to protect his client's interests.
He just did not do what needed to be done.
He could have appeared before the chambers judge to show cause why the dismissal orders should not take effect.
He did not do so.
Or he could have filed a simple notice of appeal.
Again, he did not do so.
Or he could have informed Mr.
Travis that he could not protect his interests and advise him to retain another lawyer.
He did not do this.
182 The applicant cannot distance himself from his lawyer's conduct.
183 Even if I had concluded that Mr.
Travis' trial lawyer did suffer from a medical condition that prevented him from protecting Mr.
Travis' interests, I would not have exercised my discretion in his favour.
Two reasons account for this view.
184 First, Mr.
Travis did nothing to monitor the work of his counsel in resolving what he must have understood was an immediate and pressing problem.
His lawyer never reported to him that he had dealt with the adverse dismissal decisions.
Mr.
Travis should have made pointed inquiries.
185 Second, more than six months elapsed before Mr.
Travis applied for relief under rr.
13.5(2)(a) and 14.2(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court.

With each day that passed, the weight accorded the applicant's interests in having his appeal heard on its merits diminished and the respondents' interest in having their success before the chambers judge acknowledged as final and unimpeachable increased.
By the time Mr.
Travis applied for relief, the principle of finality had long ago trumped any interest Mr.
Travis had in securing a hearing on the merits.
This court must validate the legitimacy of the respondents' belief that the actions against them were over.

34 Most recently, Burrows J, in Thistle v.

Stringam Denecky LLP, 2013 ABQB 372, after acknowledging Poundmakers Lodge, Prophet River and BA Capital Inc., rejected Master Laycock's analysis in BA Capital, which appeared to have held that the failure to account for a delay beyond six months is fatal to the application for an extension of time.
Burrows J said, and I agree, that the quality of an explanation, or its absence, is only one factor to be taken into account.
He added (at para.

19) that “[i]n a case such as this, where the delay has been short, the absence of an explanation is of much less significance than the absence of evidence of prejudice.” (The final account in that case had been sent eight months prior to the client seeking a review).
35 In addition to several of the factors listed above, Burrows J also considered, first, whether there “appears to be possible merit to the client's position that the accounts were excessive”.

While he cautioned that it is not his role to consider the actual merits, he viewed it as relevant to the exercise of his discretion to consider whether the client's complaint appears to have sufficient merit to justify a review.
This makes sense.
There is no point to this Court exercising its discretion to further an obviously hopeless cause.
Secondly, Burrows J considered whether the extension request was for a significant period of time, stating (at paras.
29-30): Where a client seeks to have an account reviewed many months after it was rendered the application should be viewed differently than where the required extension is small.
The smaller the sought extension, the easier it should be to obtain it.
This is undoubtedly related to the prejudice point previously discussed.
Prejudice to the firm's ability to defend the accounts at the review is likely to be minimal if the delay is short.
Here the sought extension is 2 months.
That is short.
36 The various factors identified in prior decisions of this Court are not watertight compartments.
(For example, Read J's factor of when the intent to tax first expressed overlaps with Master Laycock's and Rooke ACJ's factor of the reason for the delay.
Her factor of possible overcharging also overlaps with Burrows J's consideration of whether the applicant's case appears to have “possible merit”.

And, as will be seen, Burrows J's consideration of length of time of the extension overlaps somewhat with the consideration of prejudice to the lawyer.) Moreover, some of the factors may not apply in every case.

(For example, the factor of whether the parties have come to an agreement as to the amount of the account would not work in favour of or against either the Applicants or Brownlee.) All this means is that the considerations to be applied here are to be examined (as they were in Samson Cree and Prophet River) in relation to each other.

37 Taking all of the foregoing into account as well as the circumstances of this particular matter, I view the following considerations as having the most significance to deciding this application: 1.
Accounts: What sort of accounts did Brownlee render to the Applicants?
Length of Time of Extension: Is the extension sought for a short or long period of time?
Reason for Delay: Why did the Applicants fail to file their Appointments prior to the expiration of 6 months?
Prejudice: Did the delay in filing the Appointments cause prejudice to Brownlee?
Evidence of Overcharging: Is there evidence that (absent a satisfactory answer from Brownlee) might merit a finding of overcharging, such that it is just that the accounts be reviewed?
Relationship: Does the evidence of the entire relationship between Brownlee and the Applicants support an extension of time?
38 No single factor is, on its own, determinative.
For example, the absence of prejudice in and of itself would be insufficient to permit the Applicants to obtain a review of Brownlee's accounts.
(Poundmakers Lodge, at para.

18.) 39 While there is no particular order in which most of these factors should be considered, the type of accounts rendered by Brownlee is pivotal to some of the other factors (in particular the length of time extension and the reason for the delay), and so I will consider that first.
His Lordship then discussed each of the four considerations.
He said: (1)—Accounts 41 In Samson Cree (at paras.
18–43), Rooke ACJ clarified the different types of retainers that govern the lawyer-client relationship.
I will not review all of them here.
The issue to decide here is whether Brownlee's periodic accounts (being accounts that were sent out at intervals during the term of the retainer) were interim or final.
On this distinction, Rooke ACJ said (at paras.
45–46): Periodic accounts may be interim or final.

An interim account is one that is not final, but is issued pending a final account, and may be changed directly at any future time or in the end result between the time it is issued and the final account.
It is thus customary that interim accounts are not the subject of taxation individually, but rather only the final account.
When the final account is taxed, all the interim accounts issued leading to the final account are taxable.

Final accounts are ones that conclude all truly interim or provisional accounts before them (in which case, as noted, all the interim accounts are part of that taxation), or are final and taxable in themselves, with no regard to other accounts.
42 As to determining whether a periodic account is interim or final, Rooke ACJ undertook a comprehensive review of the authorities (including Sharma; Raithby v.
Fraser & Beatty (2000), 47 OR (3d) 245 (SCJ); Enterprise Rent-a-Car Co v.
Shapiro, Cohen, Andrews, Findlayson (1998), 38 OR (3d) 257 (CA); Siegel v.
Cameron & Cameron, [1996] A.J.
No.
757 (QB); Nathanson, Schachter & Thompson v.
Levitt, 2004 BCSC 1402; Poundmakers Lodge; Morin, Grant v.
Olsson (1994), 37 CPC (3d) 130 (BCSC); Siegel v.
Cameron & Cameron, [1996] A.J.
No.
757 (QB); Robertson, Ward, Suderman & Bowes v.
BC (BC Transit), (1987) 19 BCLR (2d) 1, [1988] 1 WWR 649 (CA); and Re Romer & Haslam, [1893] 2 QB 286 (CA)).
Taken together, these authorities have focussed on whether the lawyer and the client considered each of the accounts in question to be the lawyer's final account for the work recorded.

And, in determining with regard to the dealings of the parties and the circumstances whether the parties intended that each account would be final, they establish that a periodic account is likely to be considered final when the where the parties understand that the lawyer's charges will be based upon hours spent and the lawyers' billable rates, and that the charges will not be adjusted, whether upwards or downwards, upon issuance of a final bill at the conclusion of the matter. …

(2)—Length of Time of Extension 47 While the fact that each of Brownlee's accounts was a final account does not weigh against granting any extension of time, it does mean Rule 647's six month time period runs separately from the time each separate account was sent.
Consequently, the length of the necessary extension of time varies with each account ….
(3)—Reason for Delay 48 There ought to be a very good reason supporting any extension of time for seeking a review of lawyers' charges, consistent with the values which underlie the six month rule.

Is there some explanation as to why, in six months, the Applicants could not have formed and stated their concerns. … (4)—Prejudice … 64 In short, a rebuttable presumption of prejudice arises in the face of inordinate delay.
Two issues arise from this: first, whether the Applicants' delay was inordinate; and, second, whether they have rebutted the presumed prejudice to Brownlee.
65 In Samson Cree (at para.
201), Rooke ACJ held that, generally, a review of lawyers' charges initiated within the two year limitation period is not prejudicial.
This necessarily means that, in Rooke ACJ's view, a delay of less than two years is not inordinate.
The Associate Chief Justice relied upon the decision of Slatter J (as he then was) in Sharma, where he said (at para.
36): The purpose of a statute of limitations is to prevent the prosecution of stale claims.
The principle is that persons with claims should not sleep on them, and if they do sleep on them then the claims will be barred.
Potential defendants are entitled to know that, after a certain period of time, dated claims will not be pursued against them, and they can conduct their affairs accordingly: …James H.
Meek, Jr.
Trust v.
San Juan Resources Inc.., [2005] A.J.
No.
1754, 2005 ABCA 448 at para.
Once a client is served with an Appointment for Taxation, the client knows that the lawyer is seeking payment.
The Appointment starts a chain of events leading to a remedial order.
Taxation is a “civil procedure”.
As long as the Appointment is issued within two years of the original debt, then the claim is not seen as being stale by the law of limitations.
The mere fact that the enforcement proceedings are started by an Appointment for Taxation, as opposed to a Statement of Claim, should not make any difference.
The lawyer has commenced enforcement of the claim within the period provided for by the limitations statute, and the client is aware within that period that the claim is being advanced.
The purposes of the Limitations Act are met.
There is nothing in the wording of the Act to require a proceeding commenced by a more formal or traditional process.

66 With great respect to Rooke ACJ, I do not take this passage from Slatter J's reasons as speaking of prejudice, but rather of whether the taking out of a Notice for Appointment of Taxation is a remedial order within the meaning of the Limitations Act, and is therefore subject to the two year statutory limitation period.

67 If I am wrong about that, I nonetheless find myself in respectful disagreement with the general statement in Samson Cree that a review of lawyers' charges initiated within the two year limitation period is not prejudicial.
It must be remembered that the Limitations Act already precludes a review of lawyers' charges incurred more than two years prior to the client seeking a review.
(Sharma, at paras.

If, therefore, prejudice is a factor to be considered on an application to extend the time for reviewing a lawyer's charges (and Poundmakers Lodge, Prophet River and Samson Cree state that it is), then it must contemplate that such prejudice will always arise within the two year statutory limitation period.
Otherwise, any consideration of prejudice would be otiose. …

(5)—Evidence of Overcharging 72 This factor, which as mentioned was emphasized by Burrows J in Thistle, requires me to consider whether there is evidence that might merit a finding of overcharging, such that it is just that the accounts be reviewed.
The Applicants emphasize, in keeping with Burrows J's direction in Thistle (at para.

26), that they are not seeking from me a determination of whether Brownlee's accounts are reasonable or not, but the opportunity to have a review officer make that determination. … 75 Re Thompson's[Re Thompson
(1867), 2 Chy Chmbrs 100] threshold of “gross overcharge” does not bind me, nor do I take it as stating the law of Alberta.

The central question for the purpose of considering this factor is not how much a client may or may not have been overcharged, but whether there is evidence that might merit a finding of overcharging.

I agree with Brownlee, however, that this process (of the Applicants seeking an extension of time) entitles Brownlee to remain silent without fear of an adverse inference as to the merits of the complaint about overcharging.
That silence, however, requires the Court to apply this factor without the benefit of Brownlee's explanation. …
(6)—Relationship 76 Does the evidence of the entire relationship between Brownlee and the Applicants support an extension of time?
77 As a starting point, I must bear in mind that the relationship under consideration here is the lawyer-client relationship.
As such, it presupposes that some degree of trust is reposed in the lawyer (although the degree will differ among lawyer-client relationships.
See Galambos v.
Perez, 2009 SCC 48 at para.
Indeed, that trust is why clients such as the Applicants retain lawyers.
(Adams v.
Law Society of Alberta, 2000 ABCA 240 at para.

10.) 78 Rule 647(d) of the Old Rules, and its successor Rules 10.10(2) and 13.5(2)(a) of the Rules of Court, therefore presuppose that the relationship between the parties is characterized by the client's trust in the lawyer's qualities, including his or her integrity.
This characteristic must inform any analysis under these particular rules; that is, the relationship is inherently built upon the client's trust in the lawyer's integrity.

At the same time, because this characteristic is inherent (albeit to differing degrees) in every lawyer-client relationship, I must in weighing this factor also look to the qualities of this particular lawyer-client relationship.
Special Circumstances In Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
L.R.
69, McGillivray J.A. after setting out the above rules considered several conflicting English decisions.
He quoted from a judgment of Brett M.R. who had stated in Re Manchester Economic Building Society (1883), 24 Ch.
D.

488 at 497: I know of no other rule than this, that the Court has power to give the special leave, and exercising its judicial discretion is bound to give the special leave, if justice requires that that leave should be given.
The cases which were brought before the Court were cases in which either justice did require that the leave should be given or justice required that it should not be given.
McGillivray J.A. then continued at p.

346: I think that the view of Brett, M.R. is to be preferred to that of James, L.J. but whatever may be said as to the conflicting decisions under the special language of the English Rule I think that it can be laid down that under our Rules this Court considers that it has a free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case.
This division has relieved an applicant from its failure to comply with any of the four matters noted if there are special circumstances entitling the applicant to relief.
To simply lay down that the court will extend the time to appeal when the justice of the situation so requires gives little help to members of the bar in deciding how to advise a client.

This division considers it more advantageous to require an applicant to direct his attention to the four matters specified than to lay down as a general rule that time will be extended when the justice of the situation requires.
Royal Bank v.
Morin (1977), 4 Alta.
L.R.
In Stoddard v.
Montague (2006), 412 A.R.
88 (Alta.
C.A.), the Court re-affirmed the above position, and said, at p.
91: Generally, the applicant must meet all four criteria.

However, if there are “unique and special circumstances” and it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court may “excuse compliance with one or more of the criteria” and exercise its discretion to grant the extension in any event.… 6. “Prejudice” Must Relate to Extension Sought We are all of the view that this appeal must be dismissed.
Counsel for Mr.
Grotski has referred us to the decisions of this court in Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
335, and Royal Bank of Canada v.
Morin and Twelsey et al.
L.R.
These cases, and in particular Cairns v.
Cairns, set out the relevant considerations on an application to extend the time for appeal.
In relation to them counsel argues that Mr.

Grotski has suffered prejudice in that the limitation period for the commencement of this action expired in 1987, three years after the action was commenced and more than three years before the order which the bank seeks to appeal.
In our view this prejudice is no greater than that suffered by any party where an extension of time to appeal is granted to the opposing party.
It is not prejudice which arises from the very short delay which resulted when the notice of appeal filed by the bank was filed in the wrong action.
Bank of Montreal v.
Grotski (1992), 120 A.R.
Evidence in Support of Application Where a party seeks a significant time extension, it is expected to give evidence to explain the delay, i.e. why prompt compliance did not occur.
Maybe it would be different if the extension sought was slight, but here the delay was over four and one-half years.
Evidence must be proper admissible evidence such as an affidavit, not mere allegations by counsel.
The cases on time extensions generally, and those on later third party notices, seem to agree on those points.
Lister v.
Calgary (City) (1997), 47 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 14 (C.A.), at 16, per curiam.
Rule 13.5 Does Not Extend Statutory Time Limits That leaves the problem of time.
Section 152(2) of the Planning Act requires that “an application for leave … shall be made … within 30 days after the issue of the order, decision, permit or approval sought to be appealed”.
That being a statutory time limit, it is trite law that the court cannot extend it, and rule 548 on extending time limits does not apply.
Houg Alberta Ltd. v.
417034 Alberta Ltd.
In Lakevold v.
Dome Petroleum Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 1, the Court of Appeal again considered the matter of using R.
548 to extend statutory time limits.
At p.
3 Lieberman J.A., speaking for the court, said: We have considered the case of Duzs v.
394, a judgment of this Division, dealing with restrictions with respect to time found in the Divorce Act.
Allen, J.A. considers Rule 458 and at pp.
397-398 says this: Rule 548 of the Rules of Court dealing with the power of the Court to enlarge or abridge time fixed for doing any act reads as follows: . . . . .
It has been held however that such a Rule does not apply where the time for appealing is fixed by statute which confers no power on the court to extend time: see Re Fair and Toronto, 65 O.L.R.
176 at 179 (C.A.), per Masten J.A.; and Re MacDonald, 23 Sask.
L.R.
327 (C.A.), per Haultain C.J.S.
I believe the principle laid down in these cases has been adopted and followed in our Court, although I am unable to find a report of an Alberta case directly in point.
In the context of the Duzs case the above comments are dicta.
We respectfully adopt this dicta as an accurate statement of the law and would apply it to the facts of this case.
In Black Diamond Land & Cattle Co. v.
Oasis Gardeners Ltd.
318 (Q.B.), Sulatycky J.
(as he then was), said at p.
320: “A court cannot alter or extend statutory deadlines unless there is express statutory permission to do so”.
However, in Walker v.
Canadian Tire Corp.

229 (Q.B.), O'Leary J. held that the procedural (not substantive) statutory time limit for filing a transcript as required in an appeal from Provincial Court—Civil Division to the Court of Queen's Bench could be extended under R.
His Lordship said at pp.

232–33: In my view, Yorkshire Trust and other cases which hold that the court cannot extend time limits imposed by statute under rule 548 or its inherent power (see Stevenson & Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, at p.
1000) have no application here where the time limit is not substantive but procedural.
In my view this court has authority, under either rule 548 or its inherent power to control its own process, to enlarge the six-month period fixed by s.
59(3) on application made before or after expiration of the time.
It is significant that s.

59(2) permits the Court of Queen's Bench, on application made “before or after the expiration of the periods fixed by subsection (1)(a) and (b)”, to extend the times within which the steps referred to in those clauses may be done.
It would be anomalous to construe subs.
(3) as permitting an extension of time only if application is made prior to its expiration.
The intention to create such an unreasonable situation cannot be attributed to the legislature.
Section 61(1) of the Act says that if an appellant fails to comply with the requirements of s.
59, “the appeal shall be dismissed”.
If any failure to comply with s.
59 compels dismissal, as subs.
(1) seems to say, the power to enlarge time given by subs.
(2) and (3) would be of no effect.
In the context of the Act, the word “shall” in s.
61(1) cannot be construed as mandatory without totally depriving s.
59(2) and (3) of significance.
It must be interpreted as permissive and, so viewed, does not exclude operation of the inherent power of the court to extend the time for completing a procedural step.
Lastly on this point, I refer to s.
75 of the Act: No proceeding is invalid for informality if there has been substantial compliance with the requirements of this Part.
This indicates that the provisions of the Act dealing with matters of form, as opposed to substance, are to be construed liberally.

To the extent that the words in question will bear such a meaning they are to be given a meaning which recognizes that litigants in the Civil Division and before this court on appeal are not usually represented by lawyers.

The object of the portion of the Act which deals with civil claims is to provide a simple and easily understood procedure for asserting and defending claims and appealing decisions of the Civil Division.
If the words of s.
59(3) and s.
61(1) were interpreted literally, they would present a trap for the unwary.
I am satisfied that the construction I have placed upon them is in accordance with the intention of the legislature and the objects of the Act.
The strength of the appeal is irrelevant on a motion to extend time.
But in ordinary appeals, the right to extend time arises only through the general time extension rule, R.
548 … On motions for security or a stay, the strength of the appeal may be relevant.
But on a motion to extend time, strength is irrelevant unless the appeal is virtually hopeless.
Levesque v.
Levesque (1992), 3 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 193 (C.A.), at 196, 197, per Côté J.A.

paragraphs.text: (1) A pleading must be (a) succinct, and (b) divided into consecutively numbered paragraphs, with dates and numbers expressed in numerals unless words or a combination of words and numerals makes the meaning clearer. (2) A pleading must state any of the following matters that are relevant: (a) the facts on which a party relies, but not the evidence by which the facts are to be proved; (b) a matter that defeats, or raises a defence to, a claim of another party; (c) the remedy claimed, including (i) the type of damages claimed, (ii) to the extent known, the amount of general and special damages claimed, or if either or both are not known, an estimate of the amount or the total amount that will be claimed, (iii) a statement of any interest claimed, including the basis for the interest, and the method of calculating the interest, and (iv) costs, including any known special costs. (3) A pleading must also include a statement of any matter on which a party intends to rely that may take another party by surprise, including, without limitation, any of the following matters: (a) breach of trust; (b) duress; (c) estoppel; (d) fraud; (e) illegality or invalidity of a contract, including the grounds; (f) malice or ill will; (g) misrepresentation; (h) payment; (i) performance; (j) release; (k) undue influence; (l) voluntary assumption of risk; (m) waiver; (n) lack of capacity or authority; (o) wilful default; (p) tender of payment; (q) a limitation period; (r) a provision of an enactment. (4) If the defendant proposes to produce evidence about the plaintiff's reputation in mitigation of damages, the defendant must include in a pleading the facts on which the defendant intends to rely.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:1 Brief Overview See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. In Barclay v. Kokiak Heating & Air Conditioning Ltd., 2019 ABQB 850, 2019 CarswellAlta 2437, Justice D. B. Nixon gave this summary of the law: [28] A pleading requires facts, not conclusions: JO v Alberta, 2012 ABQB 599 at para 137. A pleading need only include salient facts: Klemke Mining Corporation v Shell Canada Limited, 2008 ABCA 257 at para 30; see also 677960 Alberta Ltd v Petrokazakhstan Inc., 2013 ABQB 47 at para 46. It need not name the cause of action: Petrokazakhstan at para 48; see also MDI Industrial Sale Ltd v McLean, 2000 ABQB 521 at para 7. While the difference between facts and evidence is sometimes a question of degree, the general rule is that evidence is not to be pleaded: Wenzel v Nenshi, 2015 ABQB 788 at para 12. [29] While pleadings need not name a cause of action, they do govern (i.e., regulate) the evidence of action, a pleading must include every fact that would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove in order to support his or her right to a judgment: see Read v Brown (1888), 22 QBD at 128, Lord Esher M. The classical definition of a cause of action is simply a factual situation, the existence of which entitles one person to obtain from a judicial forum a remedy against another person: see Letang v Cooper, [1964] 2 All ER 929 at 934, 1 QB 232 (HL), Diplock LJ; and Consumers Glass Co Ltd v Foundation Co of Canada Ltd (1985), 1985 CanLII 159 (ON CA), 51 OR (2d) 385 at 8, 20 DLR (4th) 126 (CA). If the pleadings do not include the facts necessary to establish an entitlement to a remedy (i.e., negligence), then no cause of action exists.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.6:2 Importance of Pleadings See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.6. In Motkoski Holdings Ltd. v. Yellowhead (County), 2010 ABCA 72, 2010 CarswellAlta 403, [2010] A.J. No. 243, 474 A.R. 367, 89 R.P.R. (4th) 159, 66 B.L.R. (4th) 161, 479 W.A.C. 367, 20 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1, 49 C.E.L.R. (3d) 1, [2010] 5 W.W.R. 603, 74 C.C.L.T. (3d) 71, the Court said, at para. 20: It is necessary to note the scope of the pleadings in this case, because it is an error of law for a trial judge to decide the case on a basis that is not pleaded: Poulos v. Caravelle Holmes (1997), 49 Alta. L.R. (3d) 385 (C.A.); M.N.P. v. Babliz, 2006 ABCA 245, 64 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1, 397 A.R. 333 at paras. 7–10; Magnan v. Brandt Tractor 2008 ABCA 345, 96 Alta. L.R. (4th) 247, 440 A.R. 35 at para. 25; Peter Pond Holdings v. Shragge (2003), 22 Alta. L.R. (4th) 41 (C.A.); McDonald v. Fellows [1979] 6 W.W.R. 544, 17 A.R. 330; Rodaro v. Royal Bank of Canada, (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 74 at 93; Kalkinis v. Allstate Ins. Co. (1998), 41 O.R. (3d) 528 (C.A.); Phillips v. Ford Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. [1971 2 O.R. 637, 18 D.L.R. (3d) 641 (C.A.). In Online Constructors Ltd. v. Speers Construction Ltd., 2012 ABCA 132, 2012 CarswellAlta 815, the Court of Appeal said, at paragraph 15: 15 A finding of liability on a ground not pled is an error of law reviewable on a standard of correctness: Northey Taylor v. Casey, 2008 ABCA 149, 429 AR 302 at para 9 citing Rodaro v. Royal Bank of Canada (2002), 59 OR (3d) 74 (CA). Although the trial judge in this case ultimately found no liability, she undertook a negligent misrepresentation analysis in the absence of pleadings or argument on that issue. This Court has held that it is generally inappropriate for a trial judge to decide a case on a basis not pled by the parties: Sumner v. PCL Constructors Inc., 2011 ABCA 326, 515 AR 231 at para 26.
